title: AST codemod workers (jscodeshift)
description: Codemods rewrite code as syntax trees, not text: jscodeshift parses each file into an AST, applies a transform function, and prints the result. A swarm runs thousands of these transforms in parallel workers across a monorepo, each file processed independently, making million-file refactors a fan-out job instead of a manual slog.
method: Parse -> find nodes via matchers -> replace/build nodes -> print; workers pull file batches from a queue; results merge as a single diff set.
usage: Write the transform against a sample, dry-run on 1% of files, then fan out workers with a shared transform bundle.

demo.code:
import ast
src = 'x = 1\nprint( x )\n'
tree = ast.parse(src)
print('AST codemod: parsed', len(tree.body), 'statements; transform would rewrite Call nodes here.')
print(ast.dump(tree.body[1])[:60] + '...')

title: Parallel git worktree shards
description: A swarm needs isolation: git worktrees give each agent its own checkout of the same repo at negligible cost (shared object store). Hundreds of agents refactor different directories concurrently, each committing to its own branch, and a coordinator merges the branches with conflict triage.
method: git worktree add per agent shard; agents commit to shard branches; coordinator merges in dependency order, re-running tests at each merge.
usage: Shard by top-level directory, cap agents per shard, and merge shards in topological order of module dependencies.

demo.code:
print('worktree shard plan:')
shards = ['auth/', 'billing/', 'search/']
for i, s in enumerate(shards):
    print(f'  agent-{i}: git worktree add ../w{i} -b shard/{s.strip("/")}')
print('3 isolated checkouts, one shared object store.')

title: Codemod canary with automatic revert
description: Before the swarm touches a million files, the transform runs on a canary slice (1% of files or one service). Metrics — test pass rate, diff size, review flags — decide whether to proceed, pause, or auto-revert the canary. Bad transforms die small instead of big.
method: Canary slice -> apply -> measure (tests, lint, diff stats) -> threshold check -> proceed or git revert the canary branch.
usage: Always canary first; encode the go/no-go thresholds in the swarm controller, not in anyone's head.

title: Dependency-ordered rollout waves
description: Refactoring a monorepo all at once breaks everything; waves roll changes out in dependency order — leaf libraries first, then their consumers. Each wave is built, tested, and merged before the next starts, so failures are always attributable to one small wave.
method: Topologically sort modules; group into waves by depth; run each wave through build+test; halt the pipeline on the first red wave.
usage: Compute the module graph, emit wave assignments to the swarm scheduler, and gate each wave on green CI.

demo.code:
mods = {'app': ['lib'], 'lib': ['core'], 'core': []}
order = []
seen = set()
def visit(m):
    if m in seen: return
    seen.add(m)
    [visit(d) for d in mods[m]]
    order.append(m)
visit('app')
print('rollout waves (leaves first):', order)

title: Cross-repo API migration bots
description: When a shared library changes its API, migration bots open pull requests in every consumer repo updating call sites to the new API. The swarm coordinates hundreds of such PRs, tracks their merge state, and escalates stuck ones — API evolution as a managed fleet operation.
method: Detect call sites via code search; generate per-repo patches; open PRs with the migration codemod; track merge state in a central board; escalate stale PRs.
usage: Freeze the new API first, generate patches per repo, and give owners a deadline before the old API is removed.

demo.code:
repos = ['svc-a', 'svc-b', 'svc-c']
for r in repos:
    print(f'  PR opened: {r} — migrate old_api() -> new_api() (codemod applied)')
print('migration board: 3 open, 0 merged, 0 stale')

title: Refactor effect telemetry
description: The swarm instruments refactored code paths with telemetry — latency, error rate, call counts — and compares against pre-refactor baselines. A refactor that passes tests but doubles p99 latency is caught by telemetry, not by tests.
method: Baseline metrics snapshot before the wave; same dashboards after; statistical comparison ( Mann-Whitney or simple threshold bands); alert on regression.
usage: Snapshot baselines per wave, keep dashboards pinned during rollout, and wire alerts to the swarm controller.

demo.code:
before, after = 120, 132  # p99 ms
print(f'p99 latency: {before}ms -> {after}ms ({(after-before)/before:+.0%})')
print('verdict:', 'REGRESSION - flag wave' if after > before * 1.1 else 'within band')

title: Mutation testing of refactors
description: After the swarm rewrites code, mutation testing seeds small bugs (mutants) into the new code and checks the test suite kills them. If mutants survive, the tests are too weak to have validated the refactor — the swarm must strengthen tests before the change ships.
method: Generate mutants (operator swaps, constant changes); run the suite per mutant; kill-rate below threshold blocks the merge.
usage: Run mutation testing on refactored modules only (not the whole repo) to keep it fast; block merges under the kill-rate bar.

demo.code:
print('mutation testing gate:')
mutants = {'killed': 47, 'survived': 3}
rate = mutants['killed'] / sum(mutants.values())
print(f'  kill rate {rate:.0%} ->', 'PASS' if rate >= 0.9 else 'BLOCKED: strengthen tests')

title: Semantic diff verification
description: Text diffs lie: reordered methods look like rewrites. Semantic diffing compares program meaning — normalized ASTs, control-flow graphs, or test behavior — so the swarm can prove a refactor changed structure without changing behavior, file by file, automatically.
method: Normalize both versions (sort members, strip formatting), compare ASTs modulo allowed transforms; run the file's tests before and after and require identical outcomes.
usage: Run semantic diff as a merge gate: any behavior change fails the shard automatically.

demo.code:
import ast
a = ast.dump(ast.parse('def f():
 return 1
'))
b = ast.dump(ast.parse('def f():

    return 1
'))
print('semantic diff:', 'IDENTICAL' if a == b else 'DIFFERENT', '(formatting ignored)')
